strengths: Clear and interesting neuroscientific motivation: the paper grounds its architectural design in the predictive coding theory of brain function, building on Caucheteux et al.'s encoding-side findings and extending the investigation to the decoding direction, which is a reasonably novel angle for the fMRI-to-text decoding literature.

The preliminary predictive-coding verification experiment (Section 2) provides a sensible empirical basis (prediction score analysis, ROI selection) for the subsequent architectural choices, rather than the ROI selection being arbitrary.

The paper conducts a battery of complementary analyses beyond the main comparison table: ROI-selection ablation (None/Random/Whole/BPC), prediction-distance sweep, an ablation removing the side network, and a novel positional decoding-error/information-loss analysis, all of which converge to support the claim that the fused predictive-coding representation is responsible for the gains rather than added capacity alone (e.g., 'Whole cortex' underperforms the targeted BPC ROIs).

The paper is transparent about limitations and uses a leakage-avoiding cross-subject splitting method (from Yin et al.) rather than the possibly compromised splitting used by a prior baseline, which is a positive for methodological rigor.
Architecture and experimental settings (hyperparameters, atlas, training schedule) are described in good detail in the main text and appendix, aiding reproducibility of the described pipeline.
weaknesses: The empirical case for state-of-the-art performance rests on a single baseline (UniCoRN); two other relevant open-vocabulary fMRI-to-text systems (Tang et al., BrainLLM) are excluded due to compatibility issues, which weakens the strength of the 'current state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract/introduction.

Reported improvements are inconsistent across metrics and settings: e.g., at sequence length 20, PREDFT's BLEU-4 (0.21) is lower than UniCoRN's (0.4), and ROUGE-1 Recall is lower than UniCoRN's in two of three length settings, undermining the strength of the overall superiority claim despite BLEU-1 gains.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported for the main decoding comparison (Table 1) or the ROI-selection/ablation tables, despite the preliminary verification experiment in Section 2 using confidence intervals; it is unclear whether the reported BLEU/ROUGE differences are robust or within noise, especially given the small absolute magnitudes (e.g., BLEU-4 differences of a few tenths of a percentage point).

Absolute decoding quality remains very low (BLEU-4 under 2% in all conditions, and qualitative examples in Table 3 show largely incoherent output), so while relative gains are of scientific interest, the practical significance of the contribution is limited and this should temper claims of 'state-of-the-art decoding performance.'

Experiments are conducted on a single dataset (Narratives) and only with cross-subject splitting; the paper itself acknowledges (as a stated limitation) that per-subject splitting and additional datasets (e.g., LeBel et al., Pereira et al.) were not tested, limiting generalizability claims.
No mention of code/data release, so despite the detailed methodological description, independent reproducibility cannot be confirmed.

The causal interpretation that predictive coding specifically (rather than simply the inclusion of additional, more predictive brain-region information) drives the improvement is only partially controlled for; the 'Whole cortex' condition helps partially disentangle this, but a more rigorous causal analysis (e.g., matched ROI count/size controls, multiple random seeds for ROI selection) would strengthen the claim.

strengths: The paper grounds its architectural design in a clear neuroscientific hypothesis (predictive coding) and provides an explicit empirical verification step (Section 2) that motivates the choice of six ROIs used later in the model, giving the method a principled rather than purely engineering-driven basis.

The proposed PREDFT architecture is described in substantial technical detail (3D-CNN + FIR + Transformer encoder for spatial-temporal fMRI features, cross-attention fusion with a predictive-coding side network, custom attention masks), and implementation details (hyperparameters, atlas, splitting method) are provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

The authors are careful about a known data-leakage issue in cross-subject splitting (citing Yin et al. 2023) and adopt a leakage-avoiding split, which is a methodologically responsible choice relative to some prior work in this area.

The ablation studies are reasonably comprehensive: ROI selection (None/Random/Whole/BPC), prediction distance analysis, hyperparameter λ sweep, and an ablation removing the side network, which jointly provide converging evidence that the specific predictive-coding ROIs (rather than arbitrary brain regions) drive the improvement.

The decoding error/information-loss analysis (Appendix B) is a novel and insightful diagnostic that connects the model's behavior to the known temporal-resolution limitations of fMRI, and shows a plausible mechanism (reduced error on late-frame words) for why the predictive coding side network helps.
weaknesses: Only one baseline (UniCoRN) is compared against; other relevant SOTA models (Tang et al. 2023, BrainLLM/Ye et al. 2023) are excluded due to compatibility issues, which weakens the strength of the 'state-of-the-art' claim and leaves open whether the reported gains would hold against stronger/more recent decoders.

Absolute decoding quality remains very low (e.g., BLEU-4 under 2% for all models, and the qualitative case studies show largely incoherent output), raising questions about the practical significance of the reported improvements despite statistically higher BLEU-1/ROUGE scores.

Results are inconsistent across metrics and settings (e.g., UniCoRN outperforms PREDFT on ROUGE-1 Recall in two of three sequence-length settings, and BLEU-2/3/4 improvements are inconsistent at length=20), so the claim that PREDFT achieves 'best overall performance' is a qualitative judgment rather than a metric-uniform result.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, paired tests) is reported for the main comparison in Table 1 or the ROI ablation in Table 2, making it hard to assess whether observed differences are robust or within noise, especially given fairly small absolute score differences in several cells.

Evaluation relies solely on n-gram overlap metrics (BLEU/ROUGE); no human evaluation or semantic-similarity-based metric is used, which is a known limitation for judging the quality of naturalistic language reconstruction, particularly given how disfluent the generated examples are.

Experiments are conducted on a single dataset (Narratives), and the paper explicitly lists this as a limitation without additional validation on other fMRI-to-text corpora, limiting generalizability claims.

The core theoretical contribution builds fairly directly on an existing encoding-side finding (Caucheteux et al. 2023) by transplanting the same ROI set to a decoding architecture; while the decoding-side investigation is new, the neuroscientific insight itself is not novel, and the paper's discussion acknowledges it does not resolve the underlying interpretive debate (Antonello & Huth) about why LM representations align with brain data.

strengths: The paper grounds its architectural design in a concrete neuroscientific theory (predictive coding) and conducts a dedicated preliminary verification experiment (brain score / prediction score analysis) before building the model, which gives the approach a principled motivation rather than being purely engineering-driven.
Extensive experimentation across two datasets (LeBel's and Narratives) under both within-subject and cross-subject settings, with multiple competitive baselines (Tang's, BrainLLM, MapGuide, UniCoRN).
Careful attention to a known reproducibility pitfall in this subfield (data leakage in cross-subject splitting, as identified by prior work), and adoption of a leakage-free splitting protocol.

Rich set of supplementary analyses: ROI selection ablations, prediction length/distance sweeps, chance-level control experiments (shuffled fMRI), hyperparameter sensitivity, decoding error/positional analysis with a novel 'information loss slope' diagnostic, and qualitative case studies.
Detailed appendix with architecture diagrams, notation tables, and hyperparameters that aid reproducibility.

Honest limitations and discussion section that engages with a competing hypothesis (Antonello & Huth) about why LM activations correlate with brain data, showing scholarly awareness of alternative explanations.
weaknesses: Absolute decoding performance remains low across all models (e.g., BLEU-1 in the 20-35% range, BLEU-4 often near 0), so while PREDFT shows relative gains over baselines, the practical/semantic quality of reconstructions is still weak, as the authors' own case studies acknowledge (garbled, largely incoherent outputs).

Results are inconsistent across metrics and subjects: e.g., PREDFT sometimes narrowly loses to baselines on BERTScore, and the 'PREDFT w/o SideNet' ablation shows large, erratic swings in ROUGE1-R across subjects (e.g., 50.28 vs 24.90 in Sub-2 of Table 1 vs Table 9), raising concerns about the stability/reliability of the reported improvements rather than a clean, consistent effect of the side network.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or repeated runs are reported for the main decoding comparisons (Tables 1-2), despite fMRI decoding being a notoriously noisy setting; single-run point estimates make it hard to assess whether observed gains are robust or due to variance.

Hyperparameter λ is tuned differently per dataset/sequence length/subject (Tables 4-5), which raises the risk of overfitting to the test conditions and makes it unclear how a practitioner would select λ a priori, weakening claims of generalizability.

The automatic metrics used (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore) are explicitly noted by the authors themselves to be poor proxies for semantic fidelity in this task, yet the paper's central claims of 'outperformance' rest primarily on these metrics; the qualitative case studies suggest the actual semantic decoding quality gap between methods may be less clear-cut than the tables imply.

The architecture is fairly complex (3D-CNN/linear fMRI encoders, FIR model, dual Transformer stacks, custom attention masks) with several design choices (e.g., mask design, prediction fusion mechanism) not individually ablated, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the predictive-coding-inspired mechanism versus general capacity/architecture increases.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, which combined with the large number of appendix experiments makes it difficult for readers to isolate the core evidentiary chain supporting the central claim.

strengths: Strong neuroscientific motivation: the paper grounds its architectural design in predictive coding theory and provides a dedicated verification experiment (Section 2) that empirically supports the hypothesized brain-LM predictive alignment before building the model, which is a more principled approach than typical purely engineering-driven fMRI decoding papers.

Extensive and multi-faceted experimentation: results on two datasets (within-subject LeBel's and cross-subject Narratives), ROI ablations (Random/Whole/BPC), prediction length/distance sweeps, a chance-level control, an ablation removing the side network, a novel decoding-error positional analysis with an 'information loss slope' metric, and qualitative case studies.

Careful attention to a known methodological pitfall in the field: the paper explicitly adopts a leakage-free train/test splitting protocol for the Narratives dataset (following Yin et al., 2023) rather than the flawed cross-subject splitting used by prior work (UniCoRN), improving the validity of the cross-subject decoding claims.

The architecture (main + side network with predictive-coding attention, masked appropriately, and end-to-end joint training with a discarded side-decoder at inference) is clearly described and technically sound, with a full notation table and detailed hyperparameter/appendix documentation supporting reproducibility of the described setup.

The ROI and prediction-length/distance analyses provide a coherent narrative connecting the preliminary predictive-coding verification findings to the downstream decoding gains, strengthening the causal story rather than just reporting a black-box performance improvement.
weaknesses: Absolute decoding quality is very low across all models (BLEU-4 mostly under 2%, and case studies show largely incoherent generated text for both baselines and PREDFT), which raises doubts about whether the reported BLEU/ROUGE gains reflect meaningful improvements in actual language reconstruction versus superficial metric artifacts; the paper does not adequately grapple with this gap between quantitative gains and qualitative output quality.

Baseline comparisons are not consistent across datasets: Tang's/BrainLLM/MapGuide are only evaluated on LeBel's dataset while UniCoRN is only evaluated on Narratives, so there is no unified comparison showing how PREDFT stacks up against all baselines on the same data; this limits the strength of the 'PREDFT outperforms existing methods' claim.

PREDFT does not uniformly win across all metrics/subjects (e.g., BERTScore is often narrowly worse than MapGuide/BrainLLM, ROUGE1-R is sometimes much lower than baselines), and no variance/significance testing (multiple seeds, confidence intervals) is reported for the main decoding tables, making it hard to assess whether observed differences are robust rather than noise.

The 'PREDFT w/o SideNet' ablation shows suspicious degenerate patterns (very high ROUGE1-R but very low ROUGE1-P in several subjects), suggesting possible short/repetitive generation artifacts that are not discussed or controlled for, raising concerns about the robustness of the automatic evaluation protocol overall.

No code/data release is mentioned, which limits practical reproducibility despite the fairly detailed hyperparameter appendix; independent verification of results would require substantial re-implementation effort.

The theoretical interpretation (that gains stem specifically from 'predictive coding' rather than generic auxiliary future-word supervision or additional model capacity from the side network) is not fully disentangled — the paper acknowledges the Antonello and Huth (2024) counter-hypothesis about LM-brain alignment in the Discussion but does not design an experiment to rule it out for its own decoding gains specifically.
